opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the more underappreciated sources of evidence we have. Most of our attention goes to pre-deployment evaluations, which matter: you want to know whether a model has dangerous capabilities before it reaches millions of people. But pre-deployment evals have real limits. They're constructed by a relatively small group of people, under time pressure, trying to anticipate how a model will be used. The world is much more creative than any eval team.

When a model is out in the world, you get an enormous, diverse stream of interactions. People push it in directions nobody anticipated. They combine it with other tools, build scaffolding around it, and find capabilities that were latent but never elicited in the lab. Sometimes they discover failure modes, like sycophancy, odd persistent behaviors, or ways the model manipulates or misleads, that only show up at scale or in long, messy, real-world contexts. So observing deployed systems gives you a much richer picture of both capabilities and propensities.

There's also a scientific point. Lab evals measure what a model can do under particular conditions. What we often care about for governance is what actually happens: how much real uplift people get, how behavior shifts across populations of users, and what harms or benefits accumulate. That's an empirical question about the sociotechnical system, not just the model, and you can only answer it by watching the system operate.

That said, there are important caveats. First, it's retrospective by nature. You learn about a problem after it has occurred, which is fine for many risks but not for those where a single failure could be catastrophic or irreversible. So evals in the wild complement pre-deployment testing; they can't replace it. Second, there are serious privacy and trust questions. Monitoring how people use these systems has to be done carefully, with aggregation, appropriate access controls, and clear norms, or you erode the trust that makes the whole enterprise legitimate. Third, there's a selection problem: what gets noticed and reported isn't a random sample. Viral examples can distort our sense of what's typical.

So my overall view is that it's highly valuable, especially as an early warning system and as a reality check on our lab-based assumptions. I'd like to see more institutional infrastructure for it: incident reporting, structured ways for developers to share aggregate findings with governments and researchers, and external researchers able to study deployed systems systematically. The labs, governments, and civil society each see a different slice of reality, and pooling those observations is one of the cheapest ways to improve our collective understanding of what these systems are actually doing.

r001.rationale: It discusses real-world uplift, benefits, and user interactions, but does not identify adopters’ revealed preferences as evidence of practical usefulness.

r002.rationale: It credits diverse real-world interactions with giving a richer picture, but does not attribute external validity to actors making real investment decisions to use AI models.

r003.rationale: It mentions latent capabilities and says some problems are learned about after they occur, but does not identify evaluations in the wild as lagging indicators of capabilities models already possessed before adoption or impact.

r004.rationale: It recommends infrastructure and external study of deployed systems, but does not recommend studying early adopters to detect capabilities sooner.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's enormously valuable, and in some ways it's the thing I'd most like to see scaled up, because it addresses a fundamental limitation of the way we currently evaluate these systems.

Most of what we call evaluation today happens before deployment. You have a model, you put it in a controlled setting, you run it through a battery of tests — dangerous capability evals, benchmarks, red-teaming — and you try to form a picture of what it can do and how it behaves. That's necessary, and I don't want to disparage it. But it has a structural problem, which is that the pre-deployment environment is artificial. You're sampling from a tiny slice of the situations the model will actually encounter, and you're sampling it in a way that the model may, in some sense, be able to recognise as a test. Even setting aside the more exotic worries about models behaving differently when they think they're being evaluated, there's just the mundane fact that the distribution of real use is vastly richer than anything a lab can construct in advance. Millions of people, with their own goals, their own weird prompts, their own ways of chaining the model into other tools — you simply cannot anticipate all of that.

So "evals in the wild" — observing how the deployed system actually behaves across that real distribution — is where you discover the things you didn't know to look for. Historically that's been true of most technologies. We learned about the risks of cars and pharmaceuticals and financial instruments largely by watching them in use, not just from pre-market testing. Post-market surveillance is a mature idea in medicine for exactly this reason.

The second thing I'd say is that it changes the epistemics of the whole governance conversation. A lot of the disagreement about AI risk is a disagreement about empirical claims — does this capability actually get used for harm, do these failure modes actually show up at scale, how fast is the capability frontier moving in practice rather than on benchmarks? If you have good observational data from deployment, you can start to resolve some of those disagreements with evidence rather than with intuition and argument. That's valuable for policymakers, who need to calibrate how heavy-handed to be, and it's valuable for the labs themselves, who often have surprisingly little systematic insight into how their own products are being used.

Now, I'd put some caveats on it. The first is that observing in the wild is inherently reactive. By the time you see a harm, it has in some sense already happened. For most risks that's fine — you learn, you patch, you iterate. But for the subset of risks that are catastrophic or irreversible, you don't get to learn from the first incident, and so wild observation can never fully substitute for forward-looking evaluation. I think of them as complementary: pre-deployment evals to rule out the worst tail outcomes, in-the-wild observation to capture everything else and to continually recalibrate your threat model.

The second caveat is about privacy and incentives. Doing this well means looking at real usage, and that raises genuine questions about what's appropriate to observe, how it's aggregated, who gets access. And the labs have mixed incentives — on one hand they want to know, on the other hand what they find might be inconvenient. So I think there's a real role for structured, somewhat independent mechanisms here: incident reporting regimes, third-party access, something analogous to how aviation safety reporting works, where the information flows to a body whose job is to learn rather than to protect any particular company.

And the third thing is that we should be building the infrastructure now, while the stakes are relatively low, because the value of this kind of observation compounds. You want the monitoring, the reporting channels, the institutional habits in place before the systems become powerful enough that the lessons get expensive. If I were ranking governance interventions by cost-effectiveness, building out a serious capacity for in-the-wild evaluation would be near the top of the list. It's not glamorous, but it's the kind of thing that makes everything else — regulation, responsible scaling policies, international coordination — much better informed than it would otherwise be.

r001.rationale: The response advocates observing real-world use to learn how models behave and are used, but it does not present adopters’ revealed preferences as evidence of practical usefulness.

r002.rationale: It says real deployment covers a richer distribution than lab testing, but does not attribute that advantage to observing actors making investment decisions to use AI models.

r003.rationale: The response calls wild observation reactive because harms may have already happened, but does not identify it as lagging evidence of capabilities models possessed before adoption or observable impact.

r004.rationale: It recommends building monitoring and reporting infrastructure, but does not recommend studying early adopters to detect capabilities sooner.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re very valuable, but we need to be careful about what we infer from them. When you deploy a model, you expose it to a much wider range of situations than you can reproduce in a controlled evaluation. People find uses you hadn’t anticipated, they discover ways around safeguards, and they combine the model with other tools. So you learn about the whole system: the model, the users, and the environment it’s operating in.

But observing no serious problems isn’t necessarily strong evidence that a model is safe. Perhaps nobody has tried the relevant thing yet, or perhaps the failures are difficult to detect. And if the concern is a sufficiently consequential failure, you don’t want your first evidence of that capability to come from an actual incident.

So I’d see these observations as a complement to testing before deployment. Ideally, you deploy gradually, have good ways to notice and investigate problems, and can change course as you learn. The central question is whether the deployment lets you learn something useful while keeping the potential consequences of being surprised acceptably small.

r001.rationale: The response says deployment reveals unexpected uses, but does not propose treating adopters’ revealed preferences as evidence of practical usefulness.

r002.rationale: It attributes learning to broader situations and interactions, without identifying actors’ real investment decisions as the source of external validity.

r003.rationale: It cautions that a lack of observed problems may be uninformative, but does not say observed adoption or impact may lag capabilities the model already possessed.

r004.rationale: It recommends gradual deployment and monitoring, but does not recommend studying early adopters to detect capabilities sooner.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re a valuable complement to evaluations before deployment. Once a model is out in the world, you see it interacting with people in a much wider range of circumstances than you could anticipate in a laboratory. People discover capabilities, find ways around safeguards, and combine the model with other tools. That can teach us a lot about what the system can actually do and how people will use it.

But we should be careful about what we infer from an absence of observed problems. We might not be looking in the right places, some harmful uses may be difficult to detect, and some risks only become apparent at scale. And, of course, if the purpose of an evaluation is to establish whether deployment could be catastrophically dangerous, learning the answer through deployment is a poor strategy.

So I’d want a combination: substantial testing before deployment, a gradual and monitored release where appropriate, and mechanisms for feeding what we learn in the wild back into both the evaluations and the safeguards. The question is whether we can learn about a failure while its consequences are still limited.

r001.rationale: The response says real-world use can reveal capabilities and usage patterns, but does not treat adopters’ revealed preferences as evidence of practical usefulness.

r002.rationale: It attributes the value of in-the-wild evaluation to broader interactions and tool combinations, not to observing actors make investment decisions.

r003.rationale: It does not say observed capabilities or impacts may lag capabilities the model already had before adoption.

r004.rationale: It recommends gradual monitored release, but does not specifically recommend studying early adopters to detect capabilities sooner.
